title: Ginamos: The Philippines Preserved in Salt — Ancient Fermented Fish Tradition
author: Glenn Junsay Pansensoy
excerpt: Discover ginamos: the ancient Filipino art of salted, fermented fish preserved through time.
body: Before there were electric lights humming in the dark, before stainless steel refrigerators lined our kitchens, and long before global shipping brought foreign goods to our shores, there was only the vast, restless blue of the sea. For the coastal people of the Philippine Islands, the ocean was the beating heart of daily life. It dictated when you woke, when you worked, and whether your family ate. On good days, the tide brought abundance—nets heavy with shimmering silver catches, baskets overflowing with dilis, bulinao, tamban, and countless small fish that flashed like coins beneath the sun. Fishermen returned to shore with the confidence of men who had read the water well. Children ran toward the boats. Mothers prepared basins, knives, and salt. The whole village seemed to move with the rhythm of the tide. But that abundance carried a silent, ticking deadline. In the humid tropical heat, fresh fish spoils in hours. The same warmth that makes the archipelago fertile also accelerates decay. A catch left too long in the sun becomes soft, sour, and dangerous. The sea gave generously, but it raised an eternal question: what do you do when the harvest is more than you can eat today? The answer was born from seawater itself. The answer was salt. And from that simple element came one of the most resilient traditions in Filipino history: ginamos. Across the island chains of the Visayas and Mindanao, ginamos is the ancient art of salted, fermented fish. It begins at the shoreline with the smallest catches—dilis, bulinao, and tiny coastal fish that are often too numerous to eat immediately but too valuable to waste. The process appears simple on the surface, but it demands an intimate understanding of nature and time. Fresh fish are cleaned and layered through with salt, tossed together until every scale is coated. The fish must be fresh; salt cannot disguise decay, only transform what is still sound. The mixture is then packed tightly into heavy clay vessels, the traditional tapayan, and sealed away from the air. Then, human hands step back, and patience takes over. Weeks pass into months in the quiet dark of the jar. Inside, salt performs a delicate double act. It draws out moisture, creating a hostile environment for harmful decay, while allowing natural enzymes to slowly break down the fish. Beneficial microorganisms and enzymes work beneath the surface, transforming proteins and fats into compounds that produce the deep, savory flavor we now recognize as umami. What emerges weeks later is not spoiled food. It is food rendered immortal. This is the paradox at the heart of fermentation: what looks like deterioration is, in fact, preservation. The fish does not disappear into rot. It becomes something else—stronger in flavor, longer in life, and richer in meaning. Ginamos makes no apologies for what it is. It hits the senses immediately—sharp, intensely salty, and heavy with a pungent aroma that can fill a room. To the unaccustomed nose, it may seem overwhelming. But beneath that initial wave lies pure umami, a deep, savory bass line that makes plain steamed rice taste whole, elevates a simple piece of fried fish, and transforms a bowl of crushed tomatoes, onions, and calamansi into an unforgettable feast. In many Visayan homes, ginamos is not an accessory to the meal. It is the meal’s soul. Long before Spanish galleons ever anchored off the coasts, indigenous Filipinos were already masters of salt and time. Along the shorelines, communities harvested salt by evaporating seawater under the blazing tropical sun or boiling concentrated brine over wood fires. In some regions, salt beds were carefully tended family enterprises, passed down through generations like land, language, or surname. Salt was never just a seasoning—it was survival, trade, and currency. With salt, a generous catch during the summer could sustain a family through winter monsoons, rough seas, and failed crops. A jar of salted fish could travel where fresh fish could not. It could be stored through storms, shared with relatives in distant villages, or exchanged for rice, vegetables, cloth, and other necessities. In communities where refrigeration did not exist and transportation was slow, preservation was not a luxury. It was a form of security. Ginamos emerged directly from this instinct for food security. It was an indigenous technology passed down from parent to child, fine-tuned to local fish, local salt, and the tropical climate. Every region developed its own variations: the type of fish used, the coarseness of the salt, the length of fermentation, the addition of other ingredients, and even the shape of the jar. These differences were not accidents. They reflected local ecology, local taste, and local knowledge. It was not a recipe brought from across the ocean. It was Filipino ingenuity forged where the land meets the water. To understand ginamos is to understand that fermentation is neither magic nor accident. It is a carefully managed biological process. When salt is mixed with fresh fish, it begins to pull water out of the fish through osmosis. This lowers the moisture available to spoilage bacteria, making it difficult for dangerous microorganisms to multiply. At the same time, salt inhibits many of the microbes responsible for rapid decay. The result is an environment where harmful organisms struggle to survive, while more salt-tolerant bacteria and naturally occurring enzymes can continue their work. Over weeks and months, these enzymes break down proteins into smaller compounds, including amino acids. One of the most important of these is glutamate, the compound responsible for the savory taste known as umami. Fats also break down slowly, contributing to the depth and complexity of the final flavor. This is why properly made ginamos does not simply taste “salty.” It tastes layered. There is the immediate sharpness of salt, the distinct character of the fish, the slight acidity that may develop during fermentation, and the long, savory finish that lingers on the tongue. The jar itself matters. Traditional tapayan, made of earthenware, allow a subtle exchange with their surroundings. They are heavy, porous in ways that modern plastic is not, and capable of maintaining a stable environment for slow fermentation. A clay jar is not merely a container; it is part of the technology. Time is equally important. A shorter fermentation may produce a fresher, milder product. A longer fermentation deepens the flavor, intensifies the aroma, and creates a more complex condiment. Each family and community learns to recognize the right moment—not by reading a label, but by sight, smell, texture, and memory. When Spanish colonizers arrived in the 16th century, they encountered these rich traditions of preserved food, but they often viewed them through a lens of cultural misunderstanding. To many Europeans, fermented fish was unfamiliar, its smell alien, its appearance unsettling. They judged it not by its function, flavor, or cultural importance, but by how closely it resembled their own food. In his 1609 chronicle, Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, the Spanish administrator Antonio de Morga wrote dismissively of local fermented fish, describing it as fish that had begun to rot and smell. It was a small sentence, but it carried the weight of empire. In calling fermented fish “rot,” Morga reduced a sophisticated preservation system to decay. He saw smell but not science. He saw pungency but not skill. He saw a foreign food, but not a Filipino achievement. Nearly three centuries later, national hero José Rizal read Morga’s account and refused to let the insult stand. In his famous annotated edition of the text, Rizal set the record straight. Filipinos were not eating rot. They were enjoying bagoong and ginamos—a deliberate and sophisticated culinary tradition where fish is preserved at its peak through controlled fermentation. Rizal understood what modern science later proved. Ginamos is not decay. It is controlled transformation. His defense mattered because it was more than a dispute over food. It was a defense of Filipino dignity. Colonial narratives often portrayed indigenous practices as primitive, unhygienic, or backward. Rizal’s annotation insisted otherwise: Filipino foodways contained knowledge, intention, and intelligence. The jar of ginamos was not evidence of poverty. It was evidence of mastery. Yet as colonial rule deepened, the world around ginamos changed. Coastal towns were pulled into systems of taxation, forced labor, and colonial commerce. Salt and preserved fish were no longer just shared within communities or bartered between neighbors. They became commodities driven by markets and empire. Families who once made ginamos purely for household survival now packed jars for trade, navigating new taxes and changing economies. Salt production became regulated. Fish trading expanded. Local food systems became connected to wider commercial networks. The same jar that once represented self-sufficiency now also represented participation in a colonial economy. Still, despite centuries of foreign rule, the clay jar remained a constant in the home. Empires rose and fell. Flags changed. Languages mixed. Roads, ports, and cities transformed the coastline. But in kitchens across the Visayas and Mindanao, ginamos continued to be made. It endured because it answered a need that no ruler could abolish: the need to preserve food, feed families, and carry the taste of home through uncertain times. One of the most remarkable things about ginamos is that it is not a single, uniform product. It is a family of traditions shaped by geography, season, and local preference. In some areas, ginamos is made primarily from dilis, the tiny anchovy-like fish that arrives in dense schools near the shore. In others, it may be prepared from bulinao, tamban, or other small fish. The choice depends on what the sea provides, what is affordable, and what the community has long known how to preserve. The salt also varies. Some producers use coarse sea salt, while others use finer salt depending on availability and technique. The ratio of fish to salt, the length of fermentation, and the method of storage all influence the final result. A jar made in one coastal town may taste noticeably different from a jar made only a few islands away. Ginamos may also be prepared with additional ingredients. Some versions include other seafood, while others are seasoned or paired with local produce. These variations show that ginamos is not a frozen relic of the past. It is a living tradition, capable of adapting while retaining its essential identity. This regional diversity is part of its cultural value. To preserve ginamos is not simply to preserve one recipe. It is to preserve many local expressions of Filipino coastal life. Today, step into a home in Cebu, Bohol, Iloilo, Zamboanga, or Negros, and you will find that ginamos still holds a place of honor. It sits on the table alongside bowls of steaming white rice, slices of tart green mango, or fresh seafood off the grill. It may appear beside fried eggplant, boiled camote, roasted fish, or a simple plate of rice and tomatoes. For millions, its aroma is not off-putting. It is the comforting smell of home, family, and tradition. A Filipino living abroad may open a jar of ginamos in a small apartment thousands of kilometers from the islands and be transported instantly to a childhood kitchen. The smell may evoke a grandmother’s hands, a father returning from the sea, a market stall crowded with baskets of fish, or a rainy afternoon when rice and ginamos were enough to make the day feel complete. Food has this power. It carries memory more faithfully than photographs or letters. Ginamos is especially powerful because it is intense, distinctive, and deeply tied to place. You cannot mistake it for something generic. It tastes like a particular shoreline, a particular family, a particular way of life. Yet the modern world presents new challenges to this ancient craft. Traditional salt artisans face land conversion, rising sea levels, and competition from cheap imported salt. Salt beds that once sustained families are being converted into resorts, subdivisions, and industrial developments. Coastal erosion and changing weather patterns threaten the delicate balance required for traditional salt-making. Meanwhile, imported salt, often produced at massive scale and sold at low prices, undercuts local producers who depend on labor-intensive methods. Small-scale fishers struggle against declining catches and high fuel costs. Overfishing, destructive practices, pollution, and climate change have altered marine ecosystems. Fish that once arrived in abundance may now be scarcer, smaller, or more expensive. For communities whose food culture depends on the sea, environmental decline is not an abstract issue. It is a threat to livelihood, identity, and daily meals. Heavy earthen jars are increasingly replaced by plastic tubs. Mass-produced factory condiments crowd out artisanal production on market shelves. Younger generations may know ginamos as something bought in a bottle rather than something made by hand. The knowledge of how to choose the right fish, layer the salt properly, manage fermentation, and recognize when the jar is ready risks becoming rarer. And yet, against the odds, ginamos endures. It survives in the bustling lanes of wet markets, in rural kitchens, and in the food memories of a diaspora scattered across the globe. It survives because it is not merely a product. It is a practice. As long as there are fishers, salt makers, cooks, and families who continue to prepare and share it, ginamos remains alive. When we speak of preserving ginamos, we are not simply speaking of keeping an old recipe alive. We are speaking of protecting an entire chain of knowledge and livelihood. At one end of the chain are the fishers. They understand the tides, the seasons, the behavior of fish, and the signs of a changing sea. Their work is physically demanding and economically uncertain, yet it remains essential to coastal food systems. At the other end are the salt makers. They transform seawater into one of humanity’s oldest preservation tools. Their work requires land, sunlight, clean water, and patience. When salt beds disappear, a crucial link in the tradition disappears with them. In between are the makers of ginamos—the families and small producers who clean, salt, pack, ferment, and share the fish. Their knowledge is practical, sensory, and inherited. It cannot be fully captured in a written recipe. It lives in hands, habits, and years of experience. To lose any part of this chain is to weaken the whole tradition. Supporting local fishers, protecting salt beds, and valuing artisanal producers are therefore not merely economic policies. They are acts of cultural preservation. Ginamos is far more than a humble side dish or a salty condiment. It is a living monument to fishers who read the tides, salt makers who turn the ocean into white crystals, and ancestors who knew how to preserve abundance without electricity. It represents a philosophy of resourcefulness. Nothing from the sea should be wasted. A small fish has value. A good catch should be protected. Nature’s abundance should be honored by making it last. It also represents a philosophy of patience. In a world of instant meals, fast delivery, and immediate gratification, ginamos asks us to wait. It asks us to trust time. It reminds us that some of the most valuable things cannot be rushed. When we lose local salt beds or neglect our small-scale fishers, we don’t just lose an industry—we lose a piece of our story. We lose the knowledge of how to live with the sea rather than merely take from it. We lose the connection between coastal communities and the food on our tables. We lose a tradition that carries centuries of adaptation, survival, and cultural pride. Ginamos: the taste of patience. It is salt worked into fresh catch, time moving quietly inside an earthen jar, and the generosity of the sea preserved for hard times ahead. It predates empires, survived colonization, and continues to sustain us today. Its future relies on us—on protecting our native salt, supporting our fishers, and remembering that even the humblest dish can carry the history of an entire nation. To protect ginamos is to protect more than a flavor. It is to protect coastal livelihoods, traditional knowledge, and the right of communities to remain connected to their own food heritage. It is to recognize that cultural preservation does not only happen in museums, books, or monuments. Sometimes it happens in a kitchen, in a market, in a clay jar sealed beneath the tropical sun. Ginamos: not just food. It is memory. It is survival. It is the Philippines preserved in salt. ↑ Back to Top
